analysis.title: US Economics Midterm Elections – Divided government limits new fiscal policy
key_insights: Citi expects the November 3 midterms to produce some form of divided government, which limits prospects for major fiscal policy changes over the next two years.
The House is expected to flip from Republican to Democratic control while Trump remains president. The Senate is a closer call and could stay Republican or flip to Democratic control.
Citi expects deficits to stay elevated at about 6% of GDP in coming years, whichever party wins on Tuesday.
Two fiscal issues need to be resolved: a budget or continuing resolution to avoid a government shutdown on December 11, and a debt ceiling increase or suspension.
The next congress must reach a bipartisan agreement to avoid a shutdown at the end of September 2027.
The 'soft' debt ceiling is likely to bind in spring or summer 2027, at which point Treasury can use extraordinary measures. The 'hard' ceiling is likely reached around Q4 2027.

Trump has floated raising the debt limit through a party-line reconciliation package in the current congress. Citi calls this unlikely given time constraints and Republican opposition to a debt limit increase.

An alternative is to tie the debt ceiling increase to a government funding package with higher non-defense spending to win Democratic votes. Citi sees this as possible but unlikely, particularly if Democrats take the Senate or otherwise do well and prefer to wait for the new congress.

Citi expects the December 11 shutdown to be avoided, while the debt ceiling and September 30, 2027 funding deadline will be addressed next year, possibly 'down to the wire' with slightly looser fiscal policy.

Democrats may push to delay scheduled Medicare cuts (about $1 trillion over 10 years) and SNAP cuts (about $120 billion over 10 years) that were enacted to offset tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Fiscal policy outlook is not significantly different whether Democrats control only the House or both chambers. Citi expects the 2027 calendar-year deficit around 6% of GDP, implying relatively neutral fiscal stimulus into next year, versus the early-2026 boost from OBBBA corporate tax cuts and larger individual tax refunds.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Deficits stay elevated regardless of the election outcome, so fiscal stimulus is roughly neutral in 2027 after the early-2026 boost from OBBBA.

risk_factors: Debt ceiling negotiations in the next congress may go down to the wire, with the soft ceiling binding in spring or summer 2027 and the hard ceiling around Q4 2027.
A government shutdown is possible at the end of September 2027 if no bipartisan funding agreement is reached.
A Democratic Senate win could make a pre-year-end deal tying the debt ceiling to funding less likely.
charts_described: Figure 1 plots Polymarket-implied probabilities of Democratic control of the House and Senate from Jul-25 to Sep-26 against a 50% threshold, and shows a high probability Democrats take the House.

tension_points.bull_case: A deal tying the debt ceiling increase to a government funding package, with higher non-defense spending to win Democratic and Republican votes, could resolve both issues before the new congress.
tension_points.bear_case: Time constraints and Republican opposition make a party-line reconciliation increase unlikely. Democrats may prefer to wait for the new congress, pushing the issue to 2027 and possibly down to the wire.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A Democratic Senate win or strong Democratic election results would make a pre-year-end combined deal less likely.
